snippet.title: What Everyday Life Was Really Like in 1900s New York | Relaxing History to Fall Asleep
snippet.description:
Step back into 1900s New York and experience the real daily life of the people who built America’s most iconic city. This video explores the crowded streets, bustling factories, immigrant neighborhoods, and rapid transformation that defined early 20th century NYC.

Discover how families lived inside cramped NYC tenements, what work was like in factories and sweatshops, and how millions passed through Ellis Island hoping for a better future. From street vendors and pushcarts to elite families of Gilded Age New York, we uncover both the hardships and the opportunities of old New York.

Whether you're fascinated by New York history, researching life in 1900s NYC, or simply curious about the city’s origins, this video gives you the most vivid look at a world that shaped modern America.
#1900sNewYork #OldNYC #NYHistory #EllisIsland #GildedAge #NYCTenements #Early20thCenturyNYC

snippet.title: Stage 1: Growing up in the early 1900s - Going to School
snippet.description:
Growing up in the early 1900s - Going to School 
What was life like for ordinary working-class children living in the suburbs or on the fringes of Australian cities in the early 1900s? How different or similar was their day to yours? Step into the shoes of the Youngein children, Jim and Dolly, from Susannah Place Sydney and find out how they lived. What grade are you in? What will you do once you graduate from primary school? This may seem like a silly question as all of you will go on to high school, but in the early 1900s, many children left school when they were 12 or 13 and started working. If you were to finish formal schooling after primary school to help support your family, what do you think you would do? What sort of jobs were available to children when they graduated from primary school in the early 1900s? Find out what Jim Youngein did when he finished primary school, then see if you can find out what some of the other children of that time went on to do for work.

snippet.title: Singapore On Film: What Life Was Like During The 1900s In The Former British Colony | Timeline
snippet.description:
Singapore on Film explores the earliest footage of Singapore, dating back to 1900. The films include 'Coolie Boys' and 'Ananas', filmed more than 100 years ago by the Pathe Brothers. Much of this remarkable archive has never been seen before, and has been specially restored and digitised by the British Film Institute. 
 
This fascinating archive shows that Singapore was a multi-cultural melting-pot, but life was grindingly hard for the majority. We see coolie dockers, rickshaw pullers, Sikh policemen and child labourers. Rare films of a grand Peranakan funeral and Hindu fire-walking show scenes both familiar and unfamiliar. Newly-discovered home movies shine an intimate light into the lives of the elite.

Through interviews with historians, writers and filmmakers, we reveal stories both epic and intimate. The programmes are narrated by renowned British actress Jenny Agutter, with the archive brought vividly to life through cutting-edge graphics and an evocative, specially-composed score.

snippet.title: What Life Was REALLY Like in a 1900s New York Tenement (10 People, One Room)

Settle in as we explore everyday routines, crowded living conditions, and quiet resilience in the tenement districts of this era.

You’ll learn how families found work, shared space and resources, managed sanitation and health risks, and built community networks that shaped city life and the wider American story.

Growing up in the early 1900s - Meals 
What was life like for ordinary working-class children living in the suburbs or on the fringes of Australian cities in the early 1900s? How different or similar was their day to yours? Step into the shoes of the Youngein children, Jim and Dolly, from Susannah Place, Sydney and find out how they lived. What did you have for breakfast this morning? Do you know what you’ll have for dinner? Very likely what you’ll have for dinner tonight will be different from what you had for dinner last week. This is because nowadays most families shop at big supermarkets with a huge array of choices. What would it have been like before supermarkets and efficient transport systems, which bring food from halfway across the world to our shops? What sort of food would you have had access to, and where would you have got it from?

snippet.title: New York c.1899: Restored To Life in Amazing Footage
snippet.description:
Time travel back 124 years to experience a typical day in New York city in these restored early films made between 1886 and 1904. Colorized and upscaled to 4K 60fps using deep learning and manual techniques with added soundscapes. 

Glamourdaze breathes new life into New York at the dawn of the 20th century. Early motorized automobiles and electric trams can be seen scooting by horse-drawn carriages, which had been the mode of transport for hundreds of years. 
Vintage clothing fashion for women in the 1900s was also on the eve of a revolution. American women are fondly remembered by the term "Gibson Girl" - the vernacular for Edwardian era fashion. In this film women are still seen walking about on the New York streets long trumpet skirts, and feminine shirtwaist blouses, held in shape by corsets. The fashionable hairstyle of the day was the 'pompadour.' which became fashionable again in the 1940s and the 1980s.

Landmarks of New York in 1899 to 1904 include:

The skyscrapers of New York - Hudson River (North River.)
Interior N.Y. subway, 14th St. to 42nd St ( opened in 1904).
Broadway & Union Square, New York.
Lower Broadway.
New York City "ghetto" fish market 
New York's Lower East Side.
Panorama of the Flatiron Building.
At the Foot of the Flatiron.
Twenty-third Street, New York City.

Restoration, upscaling to 4K 60 fps and colorization by Glamourdaze. Using machine learning neural networks. Special thanks to Bo Chang and associates.
Deep Exemplar-based Video Colorization here:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.09909

The Restoration Process:

To bring old silent 16 fps footage to life, several processes are typically employed:

1. Colorization: Using advanced algorithms and manual techniques, black and white footage is meticulously colorized to recreate the original colors of the scenes. This process involves extensive research to ensure historical accuracy.

2. Upscaling: The footage is upscaled using sophisticated algorithms to increase its resolution while preserving as much detail as possible. This helps enhance the clarity and visual quality of the footage, making it more suitable for modern displays.

3. Interpolation: Interpolation techniques are applied to increase the frame rate of the footage, smoothing out motion and reducing the choppiness inherent in low frame rate silent films. This involves generating additional frames between existing frames to create a smoother, more fluid motion.

4. Adding a New Soundtrack: A new soundtrack is composed or selected to accompany the footage, adding atmosphere and depth to the viewing experience. This may include background music, sound effects, and even dialogue or narration to further immerse viewers in the historical context of the footage.

Overall, these processes combine to breathe new life into old silent footage, allowing audiences to experience the past in a more vivid and engaging manner.




All Original archive footage preserved by Library of Congress
https://www.loc.gov/collections/early-films-of-new-york-1898-to-1906/about-this-collection/

snippet.title: What It Was Like to Be a Mental Patient In the 1900s
snippet.description:
Straitjackets. Sedatives. Bars on the windows. In 1900, patients at mental hospitals in the United States faced inhumane treatment, often because doctors could not identify the cause of their melancholy or mania. Officials at psychiatric hospitals in the 1900s, known at the time as lunatic asylums or insane asylums, locked patients up against their will, with few ideas on how to properly treat their problems. As Nellie Bly witnessed when she went undercover at Bellevue Hospital in New York, patients were beaten and choked, and their living quarters often looked more like prison cells than hospital rooms.

snippet.title: Describes Her Life BEFORE 1900! How Different Was The USA Back Then?
snippet.description:
Before the telephone. Before the automobile.  Before the airplane. Before paved roads. When most people rarely traveled more than 25 miles from their homes. It was a time of horses and buggies and the early days of US mail delivery. She was 98 years old and was telling me about her life and times back in 1979 when I filmed this interview in Lancaster Pennsylvania.

For those of you who don't know, this lady is Sarah Knauss who was born in Allentown, Pennsylvania. She died in 1999 at the age of 119, becoming the verified oldest American ever. Remember, she is the OLDEST American person to have ever lived!

Please remember when you are watching this that you are watching 16mm work print outtakes from my 1979 prime time television special, The Information Society.  Unfortunately, the material that I selected as possible to be used, has been lost in my fire of 2008. This wonderful video presents what I was going to use, including a lot of irrelevant questions. I wish I had more of this. I wish I had been smart enough as a young filmmaker when I did this back in 1979 to realize the incredible history that she was so able to articulate.  The time before the radio. Certainly before television. The time when she traveled by train and trolley and horse. The time when the telephone was a device where everyone in town could hear everyone else speaking. I found this old 16mm workprint in my basement and digitized it not knowing it would be as wonderful as it is. I recorded this for a television special I was making in 1979 called “The Information Society.” You can see the entire 1 hour film on my YouTube channel by searching it although I did not use this clip in the film.

What Life Was Really Like in America in the Early 1900s might surprise you. Before smartphones, freeways, or even widespread electricity, Americans lived in a world of steam trains, factory whistles, and candlelight. In this video, we take you back to a time when the streets smelled of coal smoke, families gathered around the radio (if they had one), and every meal was made from scratch.
What was life like in 1900? For many, it meant long hours of labor, coal-heated homes, and the dream of upward mobility. Immigrants arrived in droves, cities swelled, and the country stood on the brink of innovation and unrest. While some Americans enjoyed modern comforts, millions struggled in poverty, worked dangerous jobs, and faced rigid gender and racial barriers.
Join us as we explore the gritty reality and quiet beauty of daily life during this defining moment in U.S. history. From what people wore and ate to how they worked and dreamed, What Life Was Really Like in America in the Early 1900s will leave you with a whole new appreciation for the past.

snippet.title: What Life Was Really Like in America in 1900 | A Day in the Past
snippet.description:
What was everyday life really like in America at the dawn of the 20th century?

In this video, we travel back to the year 1900 to explore how ordinary Americans lived before modern technology transformed daily life. Long before smartphones, antibiotics, electricity, or automobiles became common, life was shaped by hard physical labor, close-knit communities, and simple routines.

At the turn of the century, most Americans worked on farms, cooked over coal or wood stoves, relied on kerosene lamps for light, and traveled by horse, streetcar, or train. Cities were growing fast, fueled by immigration and industrial expansion, but they also faced overcrowding, pollution, and poor sanitation.

From household chores and food preservation to transportation, entertainment, and communication, this video paints a vivid picture of daily life in America in 1900. It’s a world that was slower, harder, and more dangerous than today — yet filled with resilience, tradition, and hope for the future.

Understanding how people lived over a century ago helps us better appreciate the comforts and conveniences of modern life.

snippet.title: What Life Was REALLY Like for a Black Sharecropper in 1900s Mississippi (Freedom Was a Lie)
snippet.description:
What Life Was REALLY Like for a Black Sharecropper in 1900s Mississippi (Freedom Was a Lie) explores working class history in early 1900s Mississippi through a quiet, documentary-style narration made as history for sleep. On Hard Lives in History, we place this story alongside broader threads of immigrant history and labor life in the United States, with careful context and a calm pace.

You’ll learn how sharecropping contracts worked, how debt and local power structures shaped daily life after emancipation, and what survival, family, and resistance could look like for Black sharecroppers in Mississippi during this period.

African American Rural Culture, 1900–1950: https://scholarworks.iu.edu/dspace/bitstreams/0135a15b-b2ec-4820-ae82-df61760d91e6/download

snippet.title: This Is How People Lived in New York in 1900 | AI Reconstruction
snippet.description:
Step back into New York City in 1900, a time when America’s greatest city was transforming at an astonishing pace. Towering skyscrapers were beginning to reshape the skyline, electric lights illuminated the streets, elevated trains thundered overhead, and millions of immigrants arrived with dreams of a better life.

But beyond the city's remarkable growth lay another New York—one rarely seen in history books.

In this cinematic AI Reconstruction, you'll journey inside a crowded Lower East Side tenement and experience a single day through the eyes of an ordinary immigrant family. Wake before dawn in a cramped apartment, walk the bustling cobblestone streets, visit crowded markets, hear the sounds of horse-drawn wagons and factory whistles, and discover how millions of hardworking men, women, and children helped build one of the world's greatest cities.

From overcrowded housing and exhausting factory labor to vibrant immigrant neighborhoods filled with hope, resilience, and determination, this documentary reveals the hidden side of New York's rise at the dawn of the twentieth century.

Every scene has been carefully recreated using historical research, including census records, architectural plans, period photographs, newspapers, immigrant memoirs, reform investigations, and official city reports to bring the world of 1900 New York back to life with stunning historical accuracy.

Whether you're passionate about history, AI reconstructions, forgotten civilizations, or simply curious about everyday life in the past, this journey offers an immersive look into one of history's most fascinating cities.
